## Reading Real Pretraining Runs {#sec-ch6}

*What the Log Actually Says, What You Computed From It, and What You Still Don't Know*

### Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Classify any specific number from a training run as *configured*
  (declared ahead of time), *observed/measured* (logged from the
  running job), or *derived* (computed from one or more of the other
  two) — and state why conflating these three leads to wrong
  conclusions.
- State the exact relation between tokens, optimizer steps, global
  batch size, and sequence length for a declared logging convention,
  and use it to compute consumed tokens and consumed sequences from a
  raw log.
- Distinguish training loss from validation/evaluation loss, and a
  checkpoint's own metric from a "final model" metric, and explain why
  a sparse checkpoint schedule can miss a transient event entirely.
- Compute per-device and global throughput from a logged step time,
  and distinguish an *instantaneous* per-step reading from an
  *averaged/rolling-window* metric computed over several steps — and
  show how the second can mask an ongoing problem the first still
  reveals.
- Distinguish nominal/peak compute throughput from achieved throughput
  for a declared cluster, continuing Chapter 5's roofline and
  achieved-versus-peak framework rather than re-deriving it.
- Given a symptom in a run's telemetry (a loss spike or a throughput
  drop), generate at least two competing diagnoses consistent with the
  same observed evidence, and name the *specific additional
  measurement* that would distinguish between them — without treating
  temporal correlation between two logged signals as proof of which
  one caused the other.
- State what must hold (hardware, precision, sequence length, global
  batch size, token budget, model size, checkpoint position, and
  evaluation protocol) before two real runs' numbers can be compared
  directly, and recognize when a comparison should be declined or
  explicitly flagged instead of smoothed over.

### Why this matters

Chapters 1 through 5 gave you mechanisms: what next-token prediction
and multi-token prediction actually optimize, how compute-optimal
scaling and learning-rate schedules work, how data/tensor/pipeline/
expert parallelism replicate and shard work across devices, and how to
turn a parallelism configuration into a memory and communication-time
estimate. None of that preparation tells you, by itself, how to read
an actual run. In practice you are handed a log file or a dashboard: a
column of step numbers, a loss curve with a bump in it, a tokens/second
readout, maybe a technical report's own disclosed batch-size and
learning-rate schedule. The gap between "I understand how a ZeRO-3
all-gather works" and "I can tell, from this specific run's own
numbers, whether a reported symptom is explained by an optimizer issue
or a bad data shard" is exactly this chapter's subject. This chapter
does not reteach any mechanism from Chapters 1-5 — it teaches the
discipline of reading telemetry that those mechanisms produce.

### Mental model or analogy

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy"}
Treat a run's log like a patient's hospital chart. Vital signs
(observed telemetry — loss, step time, gradient norm) are not
themselves a diagnosis. A derived quantity (e.g. heart-rate
variability, computed *from* a sequence of heartbeat readings) is not
something a sensor reports directly — it is computed from observed
readings, exactly like tokens/second is computed from a logged step
time. A chart from one patient cannot be compared to another's without
accounting for age, weight, and condition — exactly the comparability
controls a run-to-run comparison needs. And two different underlying
conditions can produce the same vital-sign pattern: ordering the right
follow-up test, not staring harder at the existing chart, is what
actually tells them apart. **Where this breaks down:** a hospital can
always draw a new blood sample from the same patient to resolve an
ambiguous chart. A training run's *past* steps cannot be
re-instrumented after the fact — if a critical signal was never
logged, no amount of correlation-hunting over the columns that *were*
logged will recover it. The only remedies are logging it going
forward, or reasoning from what the existing log structurally can and
cannot distinguish.
:::

### Technical core

**Three kinds of number, not two.** Every quantity attached to a
training run is one of exactly three kinds. A **configured** quantity
is declared before the run starts and does not change on its own:
global batch size, sequence length, device count, the learning-rate
schedule's own formula. An **observed/measured** quantity is logged
*from* the running job: a step's training loss, its gradient norm, its
wall-clock step time, a periodic evaluation loss. A **derived**
quantity is computed *from* configured and/or observed values, never
logged directly: tokens consumed so far, tokens/second, model FLOP
utilization, a deviation from a trailing average. Treating a derived
number as if it had been measured directly (or a configured number as
if it had been observed) is the single most common way a reader
misreads a dashboard. This chapter's own worked example below is built
so that every number is explicitly tagged as one of these three kinds,
and every derived number's formula is stated, not assumed.

**Tokens, sequences, steps, and consumed data — one declared
convention.** For a run with no gradient accumulation (one optimizer
step per logged step) and a fixed global batch size and sequence
length, the exact relation is

$$
\text{tokens per step} = \text{global\_batch\_size (sequences)} \times \text{seq\_len (tokens/sequence)} \times \text{gradient\_accumulation\_steps}
$$

and, through step $s$,

$$
\text{consumed tokens} = s \times \text{tokens per step}, \qquad \text{consumed sequences} = s \times \text{global\_batch\_size}.
$$

Gradient accumulation (several forward/backward micro-steps sharing
one optimizer update) and pipeline microbatches (Chapter 4's own
subject) are exactly the two mechanisms that can make "a step" in a
given log ambiguous between a micro-step and an optimizer step — this
chapter does not re-derive either mechanism, but any real log must
declare which one "step" means before the relation above can be
applied. "Samples" is used loosely across real logs to mean either a
document before packing or a packed sequence after packing; this
chapter's own convention (and its worked example below) always means
the packed sequence, declared explicitly rather than left implicit.

**Training loss versus validation/evaluation loss.** Training loss is
computed on the current training batch, immediately before that
batch's gradient update — it is a per-step, per-batch, potentially
noisy quantity, and the model has not been evaluated so much as
"scored while being updated." Validation/evaluation loss is computed
on a held-out set the optimizer never updates against, typically on a
much sparser schedule (e.g. only at designated checkpoint steps) —
it is the quantity that actually estimates generalization, at the cost
of being available far less often. A validation loss slightly *higher*
than the training loss around it is an expected generalization gap,
not automatically a bug.

**Checkpoint metrics versus final-model metrics.** A checkpoint's own
logged metric describes the model's state at exactly that step — no
more, no less. If evaluation only happens at a sparse set of
checkpoint steps, a transient event *between* two checkpoints can be
completely invisible in the checkpoint record, even though the
per-step training log shows it clearly. The "final model" is simply
whichever checkpoint is actually shipped or reported — usually the
last one, but only if evaluation confirms it is not worse than an
earlier checkpoint on the metric that matters; "final" and "best" are
not synonyms unless a complete evaluation record confirms they
coincide.

**Per-device versus global throughput, and instantaneous versus
averaged.** Global throughput is tokens (or sequences) per second
*for the whole job*; per-device throughput divides that by the device
count. The two are not interchangeable: global throughput staying flat
while a device count changes implies per-device throughput changed
inversely, and per-device throughput staying flat while a device count
grows implies global throughput grew — scaling claims must specify
which one they mean. Separately, *instantaneous* throughput is
computed from one single step's own logged wall-clock time;
*averaged* throughput is computed over a window of several steps (a
rolling average, or total tokens over total elapsed wall time across a
range). A rolling average is not strictly worse than an instantaneous
reading — it smooths out step-to-step jitter that is not itself
meaningful — but it necessarily lags, and once enough slow steps have
entered its own window, it can stop flagging an ongoing problem that
the instantaneous reading still shows clearly. This chapter's own
worked example below produces exactly this outcome from a declared,
fixed anomaly-detection rule, not a hand-picked anecdote.

**Nominal versus achieved FLOPs — continuing Chapter 5's roofline
framework.** Chapter 5 already established that real hardware achieves
only a fraction of its own claimed peak throughput, and that model
FLOP utilization (MFU) is a measured-versus-theoretical *ratio*, never
either quantity alone. As of the source version verified for this
workbook on 2026-09-22, the JAX scaling guide reports that "H100s and
B200s can usually only achieve around 80-85% of the claimed peak
FLOPs, while TPUs can get closer to 95% in normal use" [@src-10] —
treat these figures as that source's own workload- and
hardware-generation-specific operating heuristics for the gap between
*advertised* peak FLOPs and *measured* achieved throughput, not as
fixed properties of these hardware families. This chapter applies exactly that
distinction to a run's own derived metrics: a cluster's *nominal*
peak throughput is a declared hardware assumption (device count times
a per-device peak FLOPs/s figure); *achieved* throughput is estimated
training FLOPs for a step (Chapter 3's own $C \approx 6ND$
compute-estimate relation [@src-50;@src-51], with $D$ here equal to
that step's own tokens-per-step) divided by that step's *observed*
wall-clock time. The ratio of the two is this chapter's own
achieved-fraction-of-nominal metric, used in the worked example below
exactly as Chapter 5 used MFU: as a *derived* diagnostic signal, never
a logged one.

**Logical versus measured memory, reused, not re-derived.** Chapter 5
distinguished five kinds of memory number: logical tensor bytes, an
analytical/theoretical estimate, a framework max-allocated counter, a
framework max-reserved/allocator-level counter, and a sampled device
framebuffer reading. Reading a real run's own memory telemetry means
applying that same taxonomy — a dashboard's "peak memory" field is
almost always the fourth or fifth kind, not the first or second, and
this chapter does not reopen that distinction beyond noting that it
transfers directly to whatever memory field a real run's dashboard
happens to expose.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"If loss and gradient norm spike together, the gradient norm spike
caused the loss spike (or vice versa)."** Temporal correlation between
two *observed* signals in the same log does not establish which one
caused the other, or whether a third factor (e.g. an anomalous batch)
caused both simultaneously. Both competing diagnoses this chapter
walks through below — an optimizer/gradient-dynamics issue, and a
data-quality problem — predict a *joint* loss-and-gradient-norm spike
at the same step; the log's own two correlated columns cannot, by
themselves, tell you which produced the other. Confirming one requires
a measurement neither column provides: here, a per-parameter-group (or
per-layer) breakdown of the gradient norm, which would show a
broad-based spike under the optimizer-instability diagnosis versus a
more concentrated one under the data-quality diagnosis.
:::

**Optimization instability versus data-quality problems — one symptom,
two families of cause.** A sudden loss spike (optionally accompanied
by a gradient-norm spike) is consistent with at least two distinct
underlying problems: an **optimization instability** (the current
learning rate or optimizer state interacting badly with a locally
sharp region of the loss landscape, producing a broad-based gradient
update) or a **data-quality problem** (an anomalous, corrupted, or
mismatched batch entering training, producing an unusually hard or
malformed example). Distinguishing them is not a matter of staring
harder at the loss curve — it requires a measurement the existing log
may not contain, as the worked example below makes concrete.

**Compute bottlenecks versus communication/pipeline-bubble/
load-imbalance/straggler bottlenecks — continuing Chapter 5's
diagnosis framework.** Chapter 5 already gave the arithmetic-intensity
test for whether a step is compute-bound or bandwidth-bound, and named
pipeline bubbles, load imbalance, and stragglers as separate
throughput limiters from a bandwidth bottleneck. Reading a real run's
own sustained throughput drop means applying that same framework to
distinguish, for example, a **communication bottleneck** (a collective
operation getting slower, affecting every device roughly equally) from
a **straggler device** (one slow participant pacing an entire
synchronous collective, while every other device sits idle waiting for
it) — two causes that can produce an identical *global* step-time
symptom while requiring completely different fixes, and that the
global step-time log alone cannot distinguish between.

**Comparable versus non-comparable runs.** Two real runs' numbers can
be compared directly only if hardware, numeric precision, sequence
length, global batch size, total token/compute budget, model size,
checkpoint position, and evaluation protocol are either identical or
their differences are explicitly accounted for. The Llama 3 technical
report [@src-32] discloses, for its 405B-parameter dense model's main
pretraining stage, an AdamW optimizer with peak learning rate
$8\times10^{-5}$, a linear warmup of 8,000 steps, and a cosine decay to
$8\times10^{-7}$ over 1,200,000 steps, together with a batch-size
schedule that starts at 4M tokens (sequence length 4,096), doubles to
8M tokens (sequence length 8,192) after 252M tokens of pretraining, and
doubles again to 16M tokens after 2.87T tokens — reaching a total
pretraining corpus of 15.6T tokens, run on up to 16K H100 GPUs (drawn
from a larger 24K-GPU RoCE cluster) at an overall reported BF16 model
FLOP utilization of 38-43% [@src-32]. The same report's own Table 4
gives three *internally comparable* configurations for the same model
on the same hardware generation and precision — 8,192 GPUs (tensor
parallel degree 8, pipeline parallel degree 16, data-parallel degree
64, sequence length 8,192) at 43% MFU; 16,384 GPUs (same TP/PP, DP=128,
same sequence length) at 41% MFU; and 16,384 GPUs (TP=8, PP=16, a
context-parallel degree of 16, sequence length extended to 131,072) at
38% MFU — with the *same* 16M-token global batch held constant across
all three rows [@src-32]. This is a *valid* comparison: same model,
same hardware, same precision, with every varied axis (device count,
parallelism degrees, sequence length) named explicitly, which is
exactly why the report itself can attribute the MFU drop to specific,
named causes (a smaller per-DP-group batch at higher DP; added
context-parallel communication at the long-context stage) rather than
leaving it unexplained.

Contrast this with comparing Llama 3 405B against the DeepSeek-V3
technical report [@src-33], which discloses its own pretraining recipe
in incompatible terms on nearly every axis: a 671B-total/37B-activated
mixture-of-experts architecture (versus Llama 3's dense 405B) trained
on 2,048 H800 GPUs (versus Llama 3's up to 16K H100s) using FP8 mixed
precision for GEMM-heavy operations (versus Llama 3's BF16) with a
maximum sequence length of 4,096 during pretraining (versus Llama 3's
4,096-to-131,072 progression) and a batch-size schedule reported in
*sequences* — gradually increased from 3,072 to 15,360 over the first
469B tokens, then held constant — rather than in *tokens* the way
Llama 3's 4M/8M/16M figures are reported [@src-33]. DeepSeek-V3's total
pretraining budget is 14.8T tokens, and its own reported training-cost
accounting is in a third currency again: 180K H800-GPU-hours per
trillion tokens (3.7 days on its 2,048-GPU cluster), 2.664M GPU-hours
for the full pretraining stage, and 2.788M GPU-hours overall including
context-length extension and post-training, which the report prices
at \$5.576M assuming \$2 per GPU-hour [@src-33]. None of the two
reports' headline numbers — MFU for Llama 3, GPU-hours and dollar cost
for DeepSeek-V3 — are even measuring the same thing, let alone the
same hardware, precision, architecture, or batch-size unit; a reader
who divides one report's tokens-per-second-sounding number by the
other's without naming every one of these differences has not produced
a comparison, only a coincidence of two numbers that happen to divide.
The right response to this pair of reports is not to force a ranking
between them, but to extract what each one *validly* supports on its
own terms, and to say explicitly which axes make a direct comparison
unsound.

### Worked example

**Setup — a synthetic, illustrative training log, not a real disclosed
run.** Every number in this section comes from a script-generated,
deliberately constructed log: 30 logged optimizer steps, a global
batch size of 256 sequences, a sequence length of 4,096 tokens, 32
devices, and no gradient accumulation (1 logged step = 1 optimizer
step unambiguously). None of this describes any real model, cluster,
or training job — it is built to contain exactly two visible behavior
changes so this chapter can walk through diagnosing each one, the same
"toy configuration" discipline Chapter 5 used for its own worked
example.

**Tokens, sequences, and throughput from the raw log.** Tokens per
step is $256 \times 4{,}096 = 1{,}048{,}576$. By step 18, consumed
tokens are $18 \times 1{,}048{,}576 = 18{,}874{,}368$ and consumed
sequences are $18\times256=4{,}608$. At the run's baseline step time of
1.800 s, global throughput is $1{,}048{,}576 / 1.800 \approx 582{,}542$
tokens/second, and per-device throughput is
$582{,}542/32\approx18{,}204$ tokens/second — three different numbers
answering three different questions, none of them logged directly.

**Nominal versus achieved FLOPs for this toy cluster.** Using a toy
parameter count of 2 billion and Chapter 3's $C\approx6ND$ relation
with $D=1{,}048{,}576$ tokens per step, estimated training FLOPs per
step are $6\times2\times10^9\times1{,}048{,}576\approx1.258\times10^{16}$.
Declaring (not measuring) a toy per-device nominal peak of 400 TFLOP/s
for this 32-device cluster gives a nominal cluster peak of
$32\times4\times10^{14}=1.28\times10^{16}$ FLOPs/second. At the
baseline 1.800 s step time, achieved throughput is
$\approx6.99\times10^{15}$ FLOPs/second — about 54.6% of nominal.

**Event A — detecting a loss-and-gradient-norm spike at step 18.**
This synthetic log's step-18 entry reports train_loss = 4.350 and grad_norm =
3.950, both well above their smoothly decreasing trend over the
preceding steps, while step_time stays exactly at the 1.800 s baseline
— ruling out a throughput event as the cause of anything unusual at
this step. Comparing step 18's loss against the trailing average of
the four steps immediately before it (3.259) gives a relative
deviation of +33.5% — comfortably past this chapter's own declared
20% anomaly threshold, so the run's own derived anomaly flag correctly
fires at step 18 and nowhere else. **Two competing diagnoses** fit this
same evidence equally well: (A) an *optimization instability* — the
current learning rate interacting badly with a locally sharp region of
the loss landscape, producing a broad-based gradient-norm spike across
most parameter groups, with loss rising as a direct consequence; or
(B) a *data-quality problem* — an anomalous or corrupted batch (e.g.
duplicated, truncated, or mixed-up tokens) producing an unusually hard
or malformed training example, with a large gradient concentrated in a
smaller subset of parameter groups, unrelated to the optimizer's own
dynamics. This log's learning-rate column is smooth and unremarkable
at step 18 (it follows the same declared linear schedule throughout,
with no scheduled change at this step), which rules out "a scheduled
learning-rate change" as a third, simpler explanation — but it does
not, by itself, distinguish diagnosis (A) from diagnosis (B). **The
measurement this log does not contain**: a per-parameter-group (or
per-layer) breakdown of the gradient norm. A broad-based spike across
most groups would favor the optimization-instability diagnosis; a
spike concentrated in a small subset of groups would favor the
data-quality diagnosis. This log only reports one aggregate,
whole-model gradient norm, so the two diagnoses remain open on this
evidence alone.

**Event B — a sustained throughput drop across steps 24-27.** In this
same synthetic log, starting at step 24, logged step_time jumps from the 1.800 s baseline to 2.880 s
and stays there through step 27, while train_loss and grad_norm
continue their ordinary smooth trend throughout — ruling out an
optimization event as the cause. Global throughput over these four
steps falls to $1{,}048{,}576/2.880\approx364{,}089$ tokens/second
(per-device, $\approx11{,}378$), and the achieved-fraction-of-nominal
metric falls from 54.6% to 34.1% — a derived signal that a bottleneck
is present, without on its own naming which one. **Two competing
diagnoses** again fit the same evidence: (A) a *communication
bottleneck* — a collective operation (e.g. an all-reduce or
all-gather) getting slower, affecting every device roughly equally, so
the whole step's wall-clock time rises uniformly; or (B) a *straggler
device* — one slow participant (thermal throttling, a flaky network
interface) pacing an entire synchronous step, while every other device
sits idle waiting for it. **The measurement this log does not
contain**: a per-device (per-rank) step-time or utilization breakdown.
Diagnosis (A) predicts every device showing roughly the same elevated
time; diagnosis (B) predicts one device showing a far higher time than
the rest. The log as given only reports one *global* step time, so it
cannot distinguish them.

**Instantaneous versus a rolling average — the same sustained event,
two different readings.** Comparing each step's step_time against the
mean of the *previous* four steps (never including the current step)
gives relative deviations of +60.0% at step 24, +39.1% at step 25,
+23.1% at step 26, and only +10.3% at step 27 — because by step 27, the
four-step trailing window itself already contains three of the four
slow steps, pulling the comparison baseline up and shrinking the
apparent deviation. Under this chapter's own declared 20% threshold,
the derived anomaly flag correctly fires at steps 24, 25, and 26 — and
then goes silent exactly at step 27, even though step 27's own
*instantaneous* step time (2.880 s) is identical to 24-26's and still
60% above the run's true 1.800 s baseline. A rolling-average-based
check and a single instantaneous reading are not interchangeable: the
averaged metric here is not wrong, but it structurally lags, and a
sustained problem can "age into" its own comparison baseline long
before it actually ends.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"If the throughput number on the dashboard looks fine, nothing is
wrong."** Depending on which throughput number — instantaneous or
averaged over a trailing window — "looks fine" can mean different
things at the same step. This chapter's own synthetic worked example
shows a trailing four-step average stop flagging a throughput drop by step 27
even while the problem that caused it (step_time still 60% above true
baseline) had not gone away. Checking only a smoothed, already-averaged
dashboard figure is not equivalent to checking the instantaneous
per-step reading, and a bottleneck that persists long enough can make
even a short rolling average "recover" on its own without the
underlying problem being fixed.
:::

**Checkpoint metrics versus the full per-step record.** This synthetic
run evaluates on a held-out set only at steps 10, 20, and 30. At step 20,
eval_loss is 3.310 against a train_loss of 3.160 — an ordinary
generalization gap, and nothing in this single checkpoint reading
hints that a loss spike happened two steps earlier, at step 18,
because by step 20 training loss had already returned to its smooth
baseline trend. A reader who only has access to the checkpoint-level
record (steps 10, 20, 30) would never see Event A at all; it is
visible only in the full per-step log. At step 30 — this run's final
logged step and the model actually used going forward — eval_loss is
3.090 against a train_loss of 2.940, the same ordinary gap, confirming
step 30 is both the final and (on this limited two-point record) the
best-performing checkpoint; a run with a non-monotonic eval curve would
need the full checkpoint history, not just the last point, before
"final" and "best" could be treated as the same checkpoint.

**Invalid configurations are rejected.** The worked example's own
script rejects a non-positive global batch size, sequence length,
device count, or gradient-accumulation count; an anomaly-detection
threshold outside $(0,1)$; a non-positive trailing-window size; a
checkpoint step outside the logged run's range; and a relative-deviation
computation against a zero trailing average — each confirmed to raise
before any of the numbers above are trusted.

### Compare and contrast

| Aspect | Observed (logged) | Derived (computed) | Example from this chapter |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tokens/sequences/steps | global_batch_size, seq_len, step index | consumed_tokens = step × tokens_per_step | 18 × 1,048,576 = 18,874,368 tokens by step 18 |
| Throughput | step_time_seconds (one step) | global and per-device tokens/second | 582,542 tok/s global, 18,204 tok/s per-device at baseline |
| Throughput, time-averaged | step_time_seconds over several steps | trailing-window average and its deviation | step 27's instantaneous reading still +60%, trailing-average deviation only +10.3% |
| Compute efficiency | step_time_seconds | achieved FLOPs/s ÷ declared nominal peak | 54.6% baseline, 34.1% during the throughput-drop event |
| Loss | train_loss (every step), eval_loss (checkpoints only) | relative deviation from trailing average | step 18: +33.5% deviation, flagged |

: Observed versus derived quantities from this chapter's own worked
example — every "Derived" column entry is computed from the
"Observed" column, never logged directly. {#tbl-observed-vs-derived}

| Aspect | Llama 3 405B main pretraining [@src-32] | DeepSeek-V3 pretraining [@src-33] | Directly comparable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Architecture | Dense, 405B parameters | MoE, 671B total / 37B activated | No — different parameter-counting convention |
| Hardware | Up to 16K H100 GPUs | 2,048 H800 GPUs | No — different accelerator generation |
| Precision | BF16 | FP8 (GEMM-heavy ops) mixed precision | No |
| Sequence length | 4,096 → 8,192 → 131,072 (staged) | 4,096 (fixed during pretraining) | No |
| Batch size unit | Tokens (4M → 8M → 16M) | Sequences (3,072 → 15,360) | No — incompatible units without conversion |
| Token budget | 15.6T tokens | 14.8T tokens | Close, but not identical |
| Headline efficiency metric | BF16 MFU (38-43%) | GPU-hours and dollar cost | No — different metric families entirely |

comparison is not valid without separately accounting for every row
above — contrast this with Table 4's own three *internally*
comparable Llama 3 configurations (same model, hardware, and

### Applied exercise

Using this chapter's own worked example as a template, repeat its
Event B walk-through for the exact same log, but now compute the
trailing-window-based throughput check using a window of 2 previous
steps instead of 4 (keeping the same 20% relative-deviation threshold
and the same declared step-time values: baseline 1.800 s, and 2.880 s
for steps 24-27). Determine which of steps 24-27 the 2-step-window
check flags versus which the original 4-step-window check flags
(steps 24, 25, and 26), and state whether a *shorter* trailing window
makes a sustained throughput drop easier or harder to keep flagging
for its full duration — and why, in terms of how quickly a shorter
window fills with already-slow steps.

### Interview lens

*"A run's dashboard shows throughput looking normal, but the team
suspects something is wrong. How do you investigate?"* A strong answer
starts by asking which throughput number the dashboard actually shows
— instantaneous or an averaged/rolling figure — since this chapter's
own worked example shows a rolling average can stop flagging a
sustained problem well before the problem itself has ended. It then
separates the three kinds of quantity this chapter distinguishes:
check the *configured* values first (did anything in the job's own
configuration actually change), then the *observed* per-step log
(not just a dashboard summary) for the actual instantaneous step
times, and only then look at *derived* metrics like achieved-FLOPs
fraction, which can reveal a drop the raw throughput number alone
might not make obvious depending on how it is computed. A complete
answer also names at least two competing causes for whatever symptom
is found (e.g. a communication regression versus a straggler device)
and states which additional measurement — not already on the
dashboard — would be needed to tell them apart, rather than guessing
from the existing numbers alone. An answer that jumps straight to "it's
probably the network" without first establishing which throughput
number was checked, and without naming a confirming measurement, is
incomplete even if the guess happens to be right.

### Chapter recap

- Every number attached to a training run is configured, observed, or
  derived — never more than one of these at once — and conflating them
  is the most common way a reader misreads a dashboard.
- Tokens, sequences, and optimizer steps relate by one declared
  convention (tokens per step = global batch size × sequence length ×
  gradient-accumulation steps); training loss and validation loss
  measure different things on different schedules; a checkpoint's
  metric describes only that checkpoint, and a sparse checkpoint
  schedule can miss a transient event the full per-step log still
  shows.
- Per-device and global throughput are different questions, and an
  averaged/rolling-window throughput metric can stop flagging a
  sustained problem well before the problem itself ends, even while
  the instantaneous per-step reading still shows it clearly.
- Nominal and achieved compute throughput are a declared assumption and
  a measured ratio, respectively — continuing Chapter 5's roofline
  framework rather than re-deriving it — and the same logical-versus-
  measured-memory taxonomy Chapter 5 introduced transfers directly to a
  real run's own memory telemetry.
- A single symptom (a loss spike, or a throughput drop) is consistent
  with more than one root cause — optimization instability versus a
  data-quality problem; a communication bottleneck versus a straggler
  device — and temporal correlation between two logged signals never by
  itself identifies which cause is responsible. Confirming one requires
  a specific measurement the existing log may not contain.
- Two real runs' numbers are comparable only once hardware, precision,
  sequence length, batch-size units, token budget, model size,
  checkpoint position, and evaluation protocol are accounted for;
  Llama 3's own internal Table 4 configurations are a valid comparison
  because every varied axis is named, while a Llama-3-versus-DeepSeek-V3
  "which is more efficient" comparison is not valid as stated, because
  none of its headline numbers even measure the same thing.
